en: Catalogue of the Scriptures, Volume One, compiled by the Sui Dynasty śramaṇas Fajing and others. Part One:
The Catalogue of the Mahāyāna Sūtra Piṭaka. This first section consists of six divisions totaling six hundred and forty-five works.
One thousand four hundred and seventy-eight fascicles. Part One: Scriptures Translated by a Single Translator. A total of one hundred thirty-three works comprising four hundred twenty-one fascicles.
*The Mahāvaipulya Buddhāvataṃsaka Sūtra*, sixty fascicles. Translated during the Yixi era of the Jin dynasty by the śramaṇa Buddhabhadra and others, together with Fayye and others, at Yangzhou.

*The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, forty fascicles. Translated during the reign of Juqu Mengxun of the Northern Liang dynasty by the śramaṇa Dharmakṣema and others, together with Huisong and others, at Guzang.

The *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*, twenty-seven fascicles, translated by Dharmakṣema at Guzang during the Northern Liang period; the *Bodhisattvamaṇyālaṃkāra Sūtra*, fourteen fascicles, translated by the śramaṇa Zhu Fonian at Chang’an in the Jianyuan era of the Former Qin;
the *Bodhisattvadṛṣṭatattvasamādhi Sūtra*, fourteen fascicles, translated by the śramaṇa Yaśas at Xiangzhou during the Tiāntǒng era of the Qi dynasty;

and the *Candrapradīpasamādhi Sūtra*, eleven fascicles, translated by Buddhabhadra at Luoyang during the Later Wei period. [The *Buddhanāmasūtra*, twelve fascicles, was translated by the śramaṇa Yaśas at Xiangzhou during the Tiāntǒng era of the Qi dynasty.]

Yaśas and Fazhi translated the *Huashou jing* (Flower Hand Sūtra) in ten fascicles at Xiangzhou. During the Hongshi era of the Later Qin, the śramaṇa Kumārajīva translated the *Shizhu duanjie jing* (Sūtra on the Ten Stages of Severing Bonds) in ten fascicles at Chang’an.

During the Jianyuan era of the Former Qin, Zhu Fonian and Dao’an translated the *Xianju jing* (Sūtra on Dwelling in Seclusion) in ten fascicles. During the Jin dynasty, the śramaṇa Dharmarakṣa translated the *Guanfo sanmei jing* (Sūtra on the Samādhi of Contemplating the Buddha) in eight fascicles.

During the Yongchu era of the Song dynasty, Buddhabhadra translated the *Jinguangming jing* (Suvarṇaprabhāsa Sūtra) in seven fascicles at Yangzhou. During the Northern Liang dynasty, Dharmakṣema [translated... [Note: The final sentence regarding Dharmakṣema is incomplete in the source text.]

The final three fascicles were translated during the Chen dynasty by Paramārtha. The *Sāgaramati-paripṛcchā-sūtra* in seven fascicles was translated by the śramaṇa Dharmakṣema at Guangzhou during the reign of Emperor Ming of the Song dynasty.

The *Dharmasaṃgīti-sūtra* in six fascicles was translated by the śramaṇa Bodhiruci at Luoyang during the Later Wei dynasty. The *Bodhisattvagarbha-sūtra* in five fascicles was translated by the śramaṇa Zhu Fonian at Chang’an during the Former Qin dynasty.

The *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra* in five fascicles was translated by Saṃghavarman and Fazhi at Xiangzhou during the Tiāntǒng era of the Qi dynasty. The *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* in five fascicles [was translated] during the Later Wei...

Śīladhara translated the *Nien-fo San-mei Ching* (Sūtra on the Samādhi of Recollecting the Buddha) in five fascicles, or perhaps six, in Luoyang. During the Daming era of the Song dynasty, the śramaṇa Guṇadeva translated the *Pao-ching Ching* (Sūtra of the Jewel Summit) in five fascicles in Yangzhou.

During the reign of Emperor Ming of the Song dynasty, the śramaṇa Dharmakṣema translated the *Ta-fang-ting Wu-hsiang Ching* (Mahāvaipulya-nirākāra-sūtra) in five fascicles, also known as the *Ta-yün Ching* (Great Cloud Sūtra), in Guangzhou.

During the Former Qin period, Zhu Fonian translated the *Ju-lai En-chih Pu-sa-i-yi Ching* (Sūtra on the Inconceivable Wisdom and Benevolence of the Tathāgata) in five fascicles in Chang’an. During the reign of Emperor Ming of the Song dynasty, the śramaṇa Dharmakṣema [continued his work] at...

The *Guhyakapuruṣa-vajra-sūtra* in five fascicles, translated by Guṇabhadra of Guangzhou; the *Mahāvaipulya-dhāraṇī-sūtra* in four fascicles, translated by Dharmarakṣa during the Taikang era of the Jin dynasty;

the *Aṅgulimālīya-sūtra* in four fascicles, translated by the Dharma-assembly at Gaochang Commandery; the *Saṃghāṭa-sūtra* in four fascicles, translated by the śramaṇa Guṇabhadra at Yangzhou during the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty;

the *Sarvabuddhaguṇavyūha-sūtra* in three fascicles, translated by Vpṛṣṇa during the Later Wei period; and the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra* in three fascicles, translated by Kumārajīva during the Hongshi era of the Later Qin dynasty, and others.

*The Sūtra on the Samādhi Asked by the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati*, three fascicles (or two fascicles), translated by Dharmarakṣa during the Jin dynasty; *The Bodhisattvapitaka Sūtra*, three fascicles, translated by Kumārajīva in the Hongshi era of the Later Qin;

*The Sūtra of Miscellaneous Dhāraṇīs*, three fascicles, translated by Dharmarakṣa during the Jin dynasty; *The Sūtra of the Fifty Calculations of the Prajñāpāramitā*, three fascicles, translated by the Anxi śramaṇa An Shigao during the Later Han dynasty;

*The Sūtra on the Samādhi of Pure Attainment*, three fascicles, translated by the śramaṇa Baoyun in Yangzhou during the Jin dynasty; *The Sūtra on the Original Acts of the Garland*, two fascicles, [translated] during the Former Qin.
*The Tathāgata’s Adornment of Wisdom Light Entering the Realms of All Buddhas*, two fascicles, translated by Zhu Fonian during the Yao Qin period.

*The Sūtra on the Intermediate State (Antarābhava)*, two fascicles, translated by Bodhiruci during the Later Wei period. *The Great Dharma Drum Sūtra*, two fascicles, translated by the śramaṇa Guṇabhadra at Yangzhou during the Song period.

*The Essential Collection of All Buddhas Sūtra*, two fascicles, translated by Dharmarakṣa during the Jin period. *The Mañjuśrī Buddha-land Adornment and Purity Sūtra*, two fascicles, translated by Dharmarakṣa during the Jin Yongjia era.
In the Xih year, Zhu Fahu translated the *Ruru Bodhisattva Anuttara-viśuddha-piṇḍapātra Sūtra* in two fascicles at Luoyang—also known as the *Jue liao zhu fa ru huanhua sanmei jing*;
translated by Kang Senghui in Nanhai, the *Bo ben jing* in two fascicles; translated by the Śramaṇa Zhi Chen during the Later Han dynasty, the *Mahāyāna-samatā-nirdeśa Sūtra* in two fascicles;

translated by the Śramaṇa Jñānagupta together with Seng’an during the Tianhe era of the Later Zhou, the *Sarvadharmāpravṛtti-nirdeśa Sūtra* in two fascicles; and translated by Kumārajīva during the Hongshi era of the Later Qin.

*The Sūtra of the Buddha Akṣobhya’s Land*, two fascicles—also titled *The Sūtra on the Bodhisattva’s Training in the Buddha-field*; alternatively one fascicle. Translated by Zhi Chen at Luoyang during the Jianhe era of the Later Han dynasty.

*The Pratyutpanna Samādhi Sūtra*, two fascicles. Translated by Zhu Fahu during the Jin dynasty. *The Kāśyapa Sūtra*, two fascicles. Translated by Yueposhouna during the Northern Wei dynasty. *The Sūtra of the Supreme Reliance*, two fascicles.

Translated by the śramaṇa Paramārtha at Guangzhou during the Chen dynasty. *The Sūtra of Unprecedented Causes and Conditions*, two fascicles. Translated by the śramaṇa Tanjing. *The Sūtra of Fierce Giving*, one fascicle.

*The Scripture on the Stage of the Path of Fierce Giving*, one fascicle; translated by Zhu Fahu during the Jin dynasty. *The Scripture of Prince Sudāna*, one fascicle; translated by the śramaṇa Faqian during the Jin dynasty.

*The Scripture of Prince Mupò*, one fascicle; translated by Zhu Fahu during the Jin dynasty. *The Scripture of King Suvarṇavarṇa*, one fascicle; translated by Dharmaruci during the Later Wei dynasty. *The Scripture of King Aśoka*, one fascicle;
translated by Guṇabhadra during the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty. *The Mahāmāyā Sūtra*, one fascicle; translated by Guṇabhadra during the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty.

*Yìfǎmén jīng* (Sūtra on the Dharma-gate of Meaning), one fascicle; translated during the Chen dynasty by Paramārtha at Fúlì Temple in Jìn'ān. *Zhízhòngdéběn jīng* (Sūtra on Planting the Roots of All Merits), one fascicle; translated during the Jin dynasty by Dharmarakṣa.

*Guānmílèshàngshēngdōushuìtiān jīng* (Sūtra on Contemplating Maitreya’s Rebirth in Tuṣita Heaven), one fascicle; translated during the Northern Liáng dynasty by Juqu Ānyáng Hóu. *Wúliàngshòuguān jīng* (Sūtra on the Contemplation of Immeasurable Life), one fascicle;

translated during the Yuánjiā era of the Song dynasty by the śramaṇa Guṇabhadra at Yángzhōu. *Guānpǔxiánpúsàxíngfǎ jīng* (Sūtra on the Method for Contemplating the Practices of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva), one fascicle; translated during the Yuánjiā era of the Song dynasty by the śramaṇa Dharmamitra.
*The Scripture on the Contemplation of the Two Bodhisattvas, Bhaiṣajyarāja and Bhaiṣajyasamudgata*, one fascicle, translated by Jñānayaśas in Yangzhou during the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty;

*The Scripture on the Contemplation of Avalokiteśvara*, one fascicle, translated by Juqu An-yang Hou at Gaochang; *The Dhāraṇī Scripture for Invoking Avalokiteśvara to Subdue and Eliminate Poisonous Harm*, one fascicle, translated by the foreign merchant Zhú Nántí during the reign of Emperor Wu of the Song dynasty;

*The Scripture on the Mantra for Repentance and the Eradication of Sin by Avalokiteśvara*, one fascicle, translated by the śramaṇa Fǎyì during the Yongming era of the Southern Qi dynasty; *The Vajra-Supreme Flavor*.

*The Dhāraṇī Sūtra*, one fascicle; translated at Luoyang during the Later Wei dynasty by Buddhayaśas. *The Sūtra on the Dharma-Door of Holding the Boundless*, one fascicle; translated during the Jin dynasty by Dharmabodhi.

*The Sūtra on the Supreme Dharma of the First Principle*, one fascicle; translated in the Xinghe era of the Later Wei by Bodhiruci. *The Sūtra of Right Reverence*, one fascicle—also titled *The Dhāraṇī of Majestic Virtue Spoken by the Buddha*;

translated during the Later Wei dynasty by Buddhayaśas. *The Sūtra of the Mother of Deer*, one fascicle; translated during the Jin dynasty by Dharmarakṣa. *The Sūtra of the Fawn*, one fascicle; translated during the Wu dynasty by... [text fragment].

*Chukong zaihuian jing* (Sutra on Eliminating Fear and Calamity), one fascicle, translated by Zhi Qian during the Xing’an era; *Famojin jing* (Sutra on the Complete Extinction of the Dharma), one fascicle—also titled *Kongji pusa suo wen jing* (Sutra Asked by the Bodhisattva Emptiness and Quiescence)—translated by the śramaṇa Bai Yan during the Wei dynasty;

*Bajixiang jing* (Sutra of the Eight Auspicious Ones), one fascicle, translated by Zhu Fahu during the Jin dynasty; *Xiaofa mojìn jing* (Minor Sutra on the Extinction of the Dharma), one fascicle, translated by Guṇabhadra at Jingzhou during the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty;
*Shiermen dafangdeng jing* (Twelve Gates Mahāvaipulya Sutra), one fascicle, translated by Zhi Qian during the Huangwu era of the Wu dynasty; *Wenshi* (The Warm Bath).

*The Scripture on Bathing the Assembly of Monks*, one fascicle; translated by Dharmarakṣa during the Jin dynasty. *The Scripture on the Four Unobtainables*, one fascicle; translated by Dharmarakṣa during the Jin dynasty.

*The Scripture on the Fields of Merit for All Virtuous Ones*, one fascicle—also known as the *Scripture on the Fields of Merit*; translated by the śramaṇas Dharmajyoti and Dharmasthiti during the Jin dynasty. *The Scripture on the Almsround of Past Buddhas*, one fascicle; translated by Dharmarakṣa during the Jin dynasty.

*The Scripture on the Merit of Leaving Home*, one fascicle; translated by Zhi Qian during the Wu dynasty. The above one hundred and thirty-three scriptures are all original texts with single translations; among them, there are none that are... [incomplete].
Since these texts have been translated individually without being divided into fascicles or chapters, yet the original versions remain intact, they should be definitively included in the canon.

2. Diverse Translations of Various Scriptures (Zhòngjīng yìyì) This section consists of two parts: (1) diverse translations of the complete versions (dàběn yìyì), and (2) diverse translations of individual chapters (biépǐn yìyì). Together, there are one hundred and ninety-five works in five hundred and thirty fascicles. *Beichuá jīng* (Sutra of the Compassionate Lotus), ten fascicles. Translated by Dharmakṣema at Guzang during the reign of Juqu Mengxun of the Northern Liang dynasty. *Dàbēi fēntuólí jīng* (Sutra of the Great Compassionate White Lotus), eight fascicles. The above two scriptures are different translations of the same original text.

The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* in seven fascicles, translated by Kumārajīva during the Hongshi era of the Later Qin; and the *Saddharma-puṇḍarīka-sūtra* in seven fascicles, translated by Dharmarakṣa during the Taikang era of the Jin. These two sūtras are the same text with different translations.

The *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* in four fascicles, translated by Guṇabhadra during the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty; and the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* in ten fascicles, translated by Bodhiruci during the Later Wei dynasty. These two sūtras are the same text with different translations.

*The Sūtra of the Bhadrakalpa*, ten fascicles—also known as the *Sūtra of the Bhadrakalpa Samādhi*, or seven fascicles—translated by Dharmarakṣa during the Yuankang era of the Jin dynasty; and the *New Sūtra of the Bhadrakalpa*, seven fascicles, translated by Kumārajīva during the Hongshi era of the Later Qin dynasty. These two sūtras are the same text with different translations.

*The Sutra on the Supernatural Transformations and the Realm of Skillful Means of the Bodhisattva*, three fascicles; *The Mahāsāṃghika-śāṭhyaputra-sūtra*, eight fascicles, translated by Bodhiruci during the Later Wei dynasty. These two sutras are different translations of the same original text.

The *Sāgaranāgarājaparipṛcchā-sūtra* in four fascicles, translated by Dharmarakṣa during the Jin dynasty; the *New Sāgaranāgarājaparipṛcchā-sūtra* in four fascicles, translated by Dharmakṣema during the Northern Liang dynasty. These two sūtras are the same text with different translations.

The *Mahādruma-kinnara-rāja-paripṛcchā-sūtra* in four fascicles, translated by Kumārajīva during the Hongshi era of the Later Qin dynasty; and the *Cundarāja-paripṛcchā-sūtra* in three fascicles (or two), translated by Dharmarakṣa during the Jianning era of the Later Han dynasty. These two sūtras are different translations of the same original text.

The *Dhāraṇīdhara-paripṛcchā-sūtra* in three fascicles, translated by Dharmarakṣa during the Jin dynasty; and the *Lokadhara-sūtra* in four fascicles, also titled the *Dharmamudrā-sūtra*, translated by Kumārajīva in the Hongshi era of the Later Qin. These two sūtras are the same original work translated differently.

*The Scripture on the Samādhi of Extensively Manifesting the Broad Way*, four fascicles; translated by Dharmarakṣa during the Yongjia era of the Jin dynasty. *The Scripture of the Dragon King Anavatapta*, two fascicles; also titled *The Request of Anavatapta to the Buddha*; translated by Dharmarakṣa during the Jin dynasty. These two scriptures are the same original work with different translations.

*The Sutra on the Samādhi of Universal Transcendence*, four fascicles, translated by Dharmarakṣa during the Taikang era of the Jin dynasty; *The Sutra of King Ajātaśatru*, two fascicles, translated by Zhi Chen during the Later Han dynasty. The above two sutras are the same text with different translations.

*The Samādhi of the Equal Accumulation of All Virtues*, two fascicles (or three fascicles), translated by Dharmarakṣa during the Jin dynasty; *The Samādhi of the Collection of All Merits and Virtues*, three fascicles. These two sūtras are different translations of the same original text.

The *Ārya-Suvikrāntavikrami-paripṛcchā-sūtra* in three fascicles, translated by Dharmaruci during the Northern Wei period; and the *Māyopama-samādhi-sūtra* in three fascicles (or two), translated by Dharmarakṣa during the Jin period. These two sūtras are different translations of the same original text.

*The Sūtra of the Devaputra Susīma*, two fascicles, translated by Dharmarakṣa during the Taishi era of the Jin dynasty; *The Sūtra of the Devaputra Susīma’s Inquiry on the Four Matters*, two fascicles, also known as the *Sūtra of the Devaputra Susīma*, translated by the śramaṇa Dharmarakṣa together with Wenhui and others in the second year of the Taishi era of the Jin dynasty. The above two sūtras are translations of the same original text.

*The Sutra on the Samādhi of the Immeasurable Treasure*, one fascicle; translated by Dharmarakṣa during the Yongjia era of the Jin dynasty. *The Sutra on the Samādhi of the Treasure Tathāgata*, two fascicles. These two sutras are different translations of the same original text.

The *Huishang púsà wèn dà shànquán jīng* (Sūtra on the Bodhisattva Prajñottara’s Inquiry into Great Skillful Means), two fascicles, translated by Zhu Fahu during the Taikang era of the Jin dynasty; and the *Dàchéng fāngbiàn jīng* (Mahāyāna Sūtra on Skillful Means), two fascicles, explained by Zhu Nanti during the Jin dynasty. These two sūtras are the same text with different translations.

The *Mañjuśrī-prabhāsa-ratnagarbha-sūtra* in two fascicles, translated by Dharmarakṣa during the Taishi era of the Jin dynasty; and the *Mahāvaipulya-ratnakaraṇḍa-sūtra* in two fascicles. These two sūtras are different translations of the same original text.

*The Sūtra of the Questions of King Veṣṭhila*, two fascicles; translated by Dharmaruci during the Later Wei period. *The Sūtra of King Īśvararāja*, two fascicles; translated by Kumārajīva in the Hongshi era of the Later Qin. The above two sūtras are the same text with different translations.

*The Sūtra on the Buddha Ascending to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to Preach the Dharma for His Mother*, Volume I (the lower volume is missing), translated by Zhu Fahu during the Taikang era of the Jin dynasty; *The Sūtra on the Infinite Transformations of the Divine Footsteps of the Way*, two volumes, translated by An Faqin during the Taikang era of the Jin dynasty. The above two sūtras are the same text with different translations.

*Chāorìmíng sānmèijīng* (Sūtra on the Samādhi of Surpassing the Radiance of the Sun), one fascicle; translated by Dharmarakṣa during the Taishi era of the Jin dynasty. *Chāorìmíng jīng* (Sūtra on Surpassing the Radiance of the Sun), two fascicles; re-translated by Nie Chengyuan during the Jin dynasty. These two sūtras above are the same text with different translations.

*Chengju guangming dingyi jing* (Sūtra on the Samādhi of Accomplished Radiance), one fascicle; translated by Zhi Yao during the reign of Emperor Ling of the Later Han. *Chengju guangming dingyi jing*, one fascicle; translated by Zhi Chen during the era of the Later Han. The two sūtras above are the same text with different translations.

*Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, one fascicle; translated by Kumārajīva during the Hongshi era of the Later Qin dynasty. *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, one fascicle; translated by Bodhiruci during the Northern Wei dynasty. The above two sūtras are the same text with different translations.

*Sūrala-sūtra*, one fascicle; alternatively titled *Sūrala-bodhisattva-sūtra*, translated by Zhi Qian during the Huangwu era of the Wu dynasty. *Sūrala-sūtra*, one fascicle, translated by Bo Yan during the Wei dynasty. The above two sūtras are the same text with different translations.

*The Mahāvaipulya Tathāgatagarbha Sūtra*, one fascicle; also known as *The Mahāvaipulya Buddha-garbha Sūtra*. Translated by Dharmakṣema and Dharmasthiti during the reign of Emperor Hui of the Jin dynasty. *The Mahāvaipulya Tathāgatagarbha Sūtra*, one fascicle. Translated by Buddhabhadra during the Yixi era of the Jin dynasty. The above two sūtras are the same text with different translations.

The *Sūtra of Immeasurable Life*, one fascicle; also known as the *Amitābha Sūtra*. Translated by Kumārajīva during the Hongshi era of the Later Qin dynasty. The *Sūtra of Immeasurable Life*, one fascicle. Translated by Guṇabhadra during the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty. The above two sūtras are translations of the same original text.

*Guangshiyin Dashizhi Shoujue Jing* (The Sutra on the Prophecy of Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta), one fascicle; translated by Zhu Fahu during the Jin dynasty. *Guanshiyin Pusa Shouji Jing* (The Sutra on the Prediction of Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara), one fascicle; translated by the śramaṇa Dharmakṣema at Yangzhou during the Song dynasty. These two sutras are the same text with different translations.

*Pumenpin jing* (Universal Gate Chapter Sutra), one fascicle; translated by Dharmarakṣa during the Taikang era of the Jin dynasty. *Pumenpin jing*, one fascicle; translated by Jīmūtavāhana during the Jin period. The above two sutras are the same text with different translations.

*The Scripture of the Old Woman*, one fascicle; also titled *The Scripture of the Old Mother*, translated by Zhi Qian during the Wu dynasty. *The Scripture of the Six Beauties of the Old Mother*, one fascicle. The two scriptures above are the same text with different translations.

*Mahāvaipulya-śikhara-rāja-sūtra*, one fascicle; also known as *Vimalakīrti-putra-praśna-sūtra*. Translated by the Śramaṇa Dharmarakṣa during the Jin Dynasty. *Mahāyāna-śikhara-rāja-sūtra*, one fascicle. The above two sūtras are the same text with different translations.

*The Sutra on Having No Expectations*, one fascicle; also known as *The Sutra on the Elephant’s Pace*, translated by Dharmarakṣa during the Jin dynasty. *The Sutra on the Elephant’s Armpit*, one fascicle. The two sutras above are the same text with different translations.
*Mahāvaipulya-sūtra*, one fascicle; translated by Dharmaruci during the Later Wei period. *Parivarta-sūtra*, one fascicle. The above two sūtras are different translations of the same original text.

*Mahāyāna-āryaprajñā-sūtra*, one fascicle; *Maitreya-paripṛcchā-sūtra*, one fascicle; translated by Dharmaruci during the Later Wei period. The above two sūtras are different translations of the same original text.

The *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-bodhicitta-sūtra*, one fascicle, also titled the *Bodhisattva-apracāra-sūtra*, translated by Kumārajīva during the Hongshi era of the Later Qin; and the *Gayāśīrṣa-sūtra*, one fascicle, translated by Bodhiruci during the Northern Wei. These two sūtras are the same text with different translations.

*The Sūtra of the High King of All Dharmas*, one fascicle; translated by Bodhiruci during the Xinghe era of the Later Wei dynasty. *The Sūtra of the Valiant King of All Dharmas*, one fascicle. These two sūtras above are the same text with different translations.

*The Sūtra on the Seal of Wisdom Samādhi*, one fascicle; also titled *The Sūtra on the Samādhi of Wisdom*, translated by Zhi Qian during the Wu dynasty. *The Sūtra on the Tathāgata’s Seal of Wisdom*, one fascicle. The two sūtras above are the same text with different translations.

*The Sutra of Decisive Compendium*, one fascicle; translated by Dharmarakṣa during the Jin dynasty. *The Sutra on Slandering the Buddha*, one fascicle; translated by Bodhiruci during the Later Wei dynasty. The above two sutras are different translations of the same original text.

*Śānta-putra Sūtra*, one fascicle; also titled *Filial Son Śānta Sūtra*, also titled *Bodhisattva Śānta Sūtra*, and also titled *Sūtra on Śānta Spoken by the Buddha*. Translated by Fa-jian during the Jin dynasty. *Śānta Original Sūtra*, one fascicle. The two sūtras above are the same text with different translations.

*The Sūtra of the Buddha Kṣīrarasmi*, one fascicle; translated by Dharmarakṣa during the Jin dynasty. *The Sūtra of the Vatsiputriya*, one fascicle. The above two sūtras are different translations of the same original text. *The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, thirty fascicles; also known as the *Dapin jing*;

translated by Kumārajīva in the Hongshi era of the Later Qin. *The Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, thirty fascicles; translated by Mokṣala together with Zhu Shulan at Cangyuan in Chenliu during the Yuankang era of the Jin. *The Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra of Radiant Praise*, ten fascicles; translated by Dharmarakṣa during the Taikang era of the Jin. The above three sūtras are different translations of the same original text.

The *Vaipulya-prabhāsa-viśuddhy-apratyudāvartana-sūtra* in six fascicles (or four fascicles), translated by the śramaṇa Zhiyan together with Baoyun during the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty; the *Avivartika-dharmacakra-sūtra* in four fascicles; and the *A-yue-wei-zhi jing* (Apratyudāvartana-sūtra) in three fascicles (or four fascicles), translated by Zhu Fahu during the Taikang era of the Jin dynasty. These three sūtras are different translations of the same original text.

A Petition Submitted to the Emperor, Compiled by the Sui Dynasty Śramaṇas Fajing and Others. The assembly of śramaṇas translating scriptures at Daxingshan Monastery, Fajing and others, respectfully address the Emperor,
our Great Donor.
On the tenth day of the fifth month of last year,
Niu Hong, the Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, received an imperial edict requiring the compilation of a catalog of the various scriptures.
We have accordingly undertaken the careful compilation of these scriptures and other texts.
In total, the various scriptures comprise two thousand two hundred and fifty-seven works,
totaling five thousand three hundred and ten fascicles; this constitutes seven volumes,
with a separate catalog in six volumes.
The *General Catalogue*, one fascicle,
has been transcribed from beginning to end.
It is hereby respectfully presented for Your Majesty’s inspection.
The Sūtras and other texts further respectfully state:
We look up with reverence to the unsurpassed Jewel of the Dharma, whose Way permeates all things without end.
During the interim of the Semblance Age, it has already been bestowed upon this land.
In the past, when Li Fangshuo beheld the ashes beneath Kunming Lake,
he was instructed to seek a definitive answer from the Western Regions; subsequently,
Liu Xiang collated the imperial library’s texts.
The *Tiangelù* records that one must have already seen Buddhist scriptures before knowing that the True Dharma had arrived long ago during the Former Han dynasty,
rather than beginning to circulate in this land only from the time of the Later Han.

However, because his Way was austere and his sentiments refined, the distinction between the true and the false was profound; few people revered him, and though he existed, it was as if he were absent.
Furthermore, this led to Emperor Ming’s dream-induced vision of the manifestation of the Golden Countenance.
It was surely because the Holy Way relied upon the Emperor and King that the grand beginning of its vast propagation was thus opened. Thereupon,
an envoy was dispatched to the Western Regions specifically to seek out Buddhist scriptures.
On this account, Kāśyapa Mātanga and Dharmaratna first produced the *Sūtra in Forty-two Sections*;
An Shigao and Lokakṣema extensively translated various other scriptural sections.
Thereafter, seekers of the Way arrived one after another.
From that time until the days of Wei and Jin in the capitals of Chang'an and Luoyang,
although Zhi Qian and Kang Senghui suddenly proclaimed the teachings in Jinling,
and Zhu Fahu and Dharmarakṣa translated them like flying torches in Yong and Luo.
However, faith and reverence were still simple, and the practice of the teachings remained meager.
By the time of the Eastern Jin and the two Qin dynasties, the sūtras and vinaya had become roughly complete;
yet, the Dharma relies on individuals for its propagation, and it was only when worthy men appeared that the light of wisdom spread widely.
Thereupon, Dharma Master Dao’an first compiled a catalog of the various scriptures.
He evaluated and categorized the materials translated during the preceding dynasties,
seeking out lost works and recovering missing texts to fully establish the formal structure of a bibliographic record.
From that time until the present, during a period of two hundred years,
there have been several dozen families of compilers who produced catalogs of the scriptures;
some sought [to organize them] by number, while others selected them by name.
Some rely on the era, while others depend on the translator;
each records but one perspective, striving to preserve their own particular view.
Only the Vinaya Master Sengyou of Yangzhou [stands apart].
The compilation of the records of the Tripiṭaka is quite worthy of inspection;
yet, the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna texts are still treated as equals, the Tripiṭaka sections are intermingled,
excerpts are collected alongside authentic transmissions, and biographical accounts are jumbled with the sūtras.
Examining the beginning and tracing to the end, none can encompass them all.
As for the various other records beyond these, how could they be fully described?

Since the monastic community has not yet been able to obtain and consult all the Tripitaka scriptures of the Three Kingdoms to verify their differences and similarities, [the task remains incomplete].
For now, relying solely upon the catalogs of various schools,
I have pruned and refined what is acceptable or rejected to establish a general framework.
This is organized into nine records, with categories clearly distinguished.
There are forty-two sections; the first six records comprise thirty-six sections.

These provide a brief indication of the distinctions between the Three Baskets (Tripitaka) of Sūtra and Vinaya, as well as the differences between the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, and offer a general manifestation of the authenticity or falsity, and the merits or defects, of the various translations.
The final three records collect biographies and commentaries.
As for the first three divisions, they were all composed by sages and worthies of the Western Regions;
because they are not the authentic scriptures of the Tripiṭaka, they are categorized as separate records.
The latter three sections were all composed by virtuous scholars of this land;
although they do not resemble those produced in the Western Regions,
they are none other than commentaries that assist and elucidate the authentic scriptures.
He elucidated the religious teachings,
illuminating the legacy of his predecessors and opening the way for future scholars.
Therefore, they have been recorded together here.
Furthermore, Fa-jing and others reflected further upon this:
the bibliographies of the various schools were for the most part compiled by worthy sages of previous dynasties.
I respectfully observe that among the former sages, there were none who did not style themselves as contemporaries investigating antiquity;
yet, the works they compiled did not reach the level of thoroughness and precision.
This was not because those worthies lacked talent or their learning was incomplete.
It was truly a time when the world was fragmented and the nine provinces were without a ruler;
famous states and great commanderies each proclaimed themselves the imperial capital.
The borders were difficult and perilous, and all were divided among the warring states.
Wherever the scriptures were found, no one knew of their existence elsewhere;
scholars heard of them from afar, yet throughout their lives never beheld them.
Therefore, although those former sages possessed talent and ability,
if they did not encounter their time, they had no means to express themselves.
At present, our understanding of the scriptures and our scholarly learning truly do not equal that of antiquity.
Yet, due to past affinities, there was much good fortune, and he encountered auspicious times.
With the four seas as his home, the six directions were clear and peaceful;
lands of different regions and diverse customs appeared as if they were right before one's eyes.
The calendar and the system of writing are disseminated so that there are no lands beyond its reach;
furthermore, Your Majesty, the Great Donor,
although you personally oversee the myriad affairs of state, [remains ever detached].
Yet, being devoted to the Way throughout his entire life, he restored the Triple Gem and became a Wheel-Turning King of the Dharma.
He forever closed the gates to the four miserable realms and grandly opened the path for devas and humans.
Within the realms of sentient beings, there is none who does not rely upon and benefit from [the Dharma], let alone the sutras and other scriptures.
What further need is there to discuss this? My only regret is that my wisdom and insight are not extensive, yet I have presumptuously participated in this auspicious enterprise.
I was unable to obtain all the scriptural texts of the Three Kingdoms, nor the surviving writings and lost teachings.
Consequently, there are many obscurities and errors in this hastily compiled work.
Reflecting on my shortcomings and reviewing my failings, I feel profound shame and regret.
